cards.heading: Definition
cards.question: What is 'disposable artifacts as specification'?
cards.answer: Having a model produce cheap, throwaway concretions — divergent mockups with fake data, a single-file prototype, a plan ordered by likely change — meant to be reacted to and discarded, because judgment people can't state in advance reliably appears once they see a candidate in front of them.

cards.heading: Key mechanism
cards.question: Why does the technique deliberately produce several divergent options rather than one?
cards.answer: Divergent options elicit preference; a single option only elicits acquiescence.

cards.heading: Economics of discovery timing
cards.question: Why is discovering a criterion against a throwaway mock cheaper than discovering it mid-implementation?
cards.answer: A small spec change can imply a drastically different implementation, and an agent that has already built the wrong thing reverts it poorly — so the same criterion costs minutes against a mock but costs the implementation if found later.

cards.heading: Code as reference
cards.question: Why is existing source code a stronger reference for desired behaviour than a screenshot or description?
cards.answer: Code carries structure and semantics rather than just appearance, even across languages.

cards.heading: Review plan ordering
cards.question: How should a review plan be ordered, and why?
cards.answer: By likelihood of change — front-loading decisions like data models, type interfaces and user-facing flows, and burying mechanical work — so review attention lands where changing your mind is still cheap.
